subject: Urban Planning
title: E-Waste: The Digital Dump
description: A quick, practical guide to E-Waste: The Digital Dump.

hook.text: The world generates 62 million tons of e-waste annually — more than the weight of the Great Wall of China.

buildup.text: Old phones, laptops, and TVs contain gold, copper, and rare earth metals. They also contain lead, mercury, and cadmium.

discovery.text: Agbogbloshie in Ghana was the world's largest e-waste dump. Workers burned electronics to extract copper, inhaling toxic fumes.

twist.text: Only 17% of e-waste is formally recycled. The rest is dumped, burned, or shipped illegally to developing countries.

climax.text: The EU's right-to-repair laws and extended producer responsibility are pushing companies to design recyclable electronics.

punchline.text: Your old phone has gold in it. Someone is burning it to get the copper out.

quiz.question: Why is e-waste both valuable and dangerous?
options: Electronics contain precious metals but also toxic substances like lead and mercury
E-waste generates electricity when burned but produces carbon dioxide
Digital data stored on devices can be stolen if not properly destroyed
